opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it was one of the most valuable things that happened to me, even though it didn't feel great at the time. When I got to FAIR, I'd spent my whole PhD on structured prediction: parsing, combinatorial optimization, dual decomposition, really thinking about the discrete structure of language. Then I showed up and suddenly everyone around me was training these big neural networks that just didn't care about any of that. They were getting results on problems I'd assumed needed all this careful machinery.

So you have two options. You can dig in and defend what you know, or you can sit with the discomfort and ask, "Okay, what am I actually wrong about here?" I tried to do the second, and it forced me to separate the things I believed for good reasons from the things I believed because they were what I'd been trained on. Some of my intuitions turned out to be wrong. Others survived, and I came to understand them better because I'd had to argue for them against people who were skeptical.

I think that's the general lesson. Early in your career it's very easy to get locked into a framing, especially if it's working and you're getting papers out of it. Being around smart people who fundamentally disagree with your assumptions is uncomfortable, but it makes you a better scientist. You either update, or you come out with a much sharper sense of why your view matters. Honestly, a lot of what I've worked on since, like trying to bring structure back into neural models in a way that actually helps, came directly from that tension. I wouldn't have gotten there if I'd stayed somewhere everyone already agreed with me.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes arriving at FAIR to find colleagues pursuing neural networks that challenged their structured-prediction focus, then sitting with the discomfort and reconsidering which of their beliefs were wrong.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's really easy, especially coming out of grad school, to get locked into a particular view of what the problems are and what the right tools are. I'd spent my PhD working on structured prediction, parsing, these very discrete, combinatorial models of language, and I had a lot of intellectual investment in that way of thinking. Then I got to FAIR right at the moment when deep learning was really taking over NLP, and I was sitting next to people who just did not care about any of the things I thought were important. They weren't interested in syntax, they weren't interested in latent structure, they just wanted to know whether the model worked.

And honestly that was uncomfortable at first. But it forced me to actually articulate why I believed what I believed, rather than just taking it as a given from my training. Some of those beliefs held up, and I think some of my later work on combining structure with neural models came directly out of having to defend them. But a lot of them didn't hold up, and I had to let them go. That's a much faster way to learn than reading papers, because people are pushing back on you in real time and you can't just ignore the critique.

So the reason I recommend it is that I think research communities, and individual researchers, tend to drift toward consensus within their own group. Being dropped into an environment where the consensus is different is one of the few things that actually reveals which of your ideas are load-bearing and which are just habits. You come out of it with a much clearer sense of what you actually think, and you're also a lot more open to being surprised, which I think is the main thing you need to do good work in a field that's moving this quickly.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the unfamiliar FAIR environment was uncomfortable and forced them to examine and abandon some established beliefs, prompting a shift in their research thinking.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s easy, as a researcher, to get attached to a particular way of framing problems. You build up expertise, you have a community that cares about the same questions, and you can start taking for granted that those are the right questions to ask.

Being at FAIR challenged that for me. You’re around people who are very smart but don’t necessarily share your assumptions about what matters or what approaches are promising. And having to explain why you care about something—to someone who isn’t already bought in—is really valuable. Sometimes you come away more convinced, and sometimes you realize that part of your motivation was just habit.

That can be uncomfortable, especially when you’ve invested years in an area. But I think it helps you separate the underlying problems you really care about from the particular methods you’ve become comfortable using.

r001.rationale: The response says that encountering people with different assumptions can prompt researchers to question their motivations and methods, but it does not clearly state that feeling intellectually out of place prompts reconsidering an established research direction.

sol-6.1.text: I think once you’ve worked on something for a while, it’s easy to take for granted that your problems are the important ones, or that your way of approaching them is the right one. Being at FAIR put me around people with very different intuitions, who were willing to question those assumptions. That can be uncomfortable—you have to explain why you care about something instead of assuming everyone agrees. But it helps you distinguish the ideas you really believe in from the things you’re doing out of habit. You don’t have to abandon your interests; you come back to them with a clearer sense of why they matter, and sometimes with a much better way to pursue them.

r001.rationale: The response says that being around people with different intuitions who question your assumptions can reveal which interests are habitual and help you return to them with a clearer sense of why they matter.
